title: Self-hosting AstaBrief-8B for cited reports: check every bracket before anyone reads it
summary:
You have search over your own documents. Next comes a report with a reference after every claim, and the Allen Institute for AI (Ai2) released AstaBrief-8B for that writing step. The weights (the trained model file you download) are Apache 2.0, and the base is the Qwen team's Qwen3-8B. We ran it on one NVIDIA RTX A5000, a 24 GB card, and counted every reference it wrote.

Serving it is easy. One check in the code around it is not optional.

Decision one: the prompt is not yours to write

Ai2 trained the model on one fixed instruction file. The model card warns that swapping it may give "degraded or inconsistent behavior". So your code fills two blanks, the question and the excerpts, and keeps even the line "Note that the current year is 2025". No report stated the wrong year; whether it ranks 2025 papers as the latest work, we left untested.

Each excerpt carries a label: an ID, the first author, the year and a citation count (how many other papers cite it). The model copies it into square brackets after each claim, and should write "(LLM Memory)" when it relies on its own recollection.

Check the licence first. Apache 2.0 covers the weights only; the instruction file is CC-BY-NC-4.0, non-commercial. A paid product must clear that licence or write its own prompt in the same format, with the risk the card describes. Our SDK example ships no copy: it fetches the file from Ai2 at run time, under Ai2's terms.

Decision two: size the context, then let it batch

vLLM, the open-source program that loads a model onto the GPU and answers requests, treats AstaBrief as an ordinary Qwen3 model, with no custom code. Text is counted in tokens, about three quarters of a word each. The weights fill 16.4 GB of the 24 GB. We capped each request at 16,384 tokens (question, excerpts and report), the length of Ai2's final training round. The leftover memory holds two requests at that cap side by side. Our real requests were nearer 7,000 tokens, so about four fit.

Alone on the card, one report took 41.5 to 64.7 s, at roughly 39 tokens a second. Sending four is more telling.

Sent together, four reports took 85 s, against 209 s one after another. The first try missed that, through a bug of ours. Concurrency is how many requests a model may work on at once, and pinning a model to one GPU machine through our SDK set it to one. The four waited in line: 198 s, and one report vanished. One settings call raises the limit today. The vanished report revealed a second, unfixed bug. If the first token (the opening piece of the answer) takes over 3 minutes, the request closes empty with no error. The card still finishes a report nobody receives. The AstaBrief-8B test notes on inferencekey.com cover both, plus the workaround.

On your stack, test the concurrency limit at each layer, first-token time under load, and whether a timeout fails loudly.

Decision three: the label check is part of the pipeline

The 11 reports held 380 references, and 363 (95.5%) match an excerpt we sent. Good, and also the trap: the other 17 look just like the genuine ones.

Eight of the 11 reports cited 1 to 3 labels the prompt never contained. Part of them were our own excerpts with the label garbled. We sent [W4411306417 | Thapliyal et al. | 2025 | Citations: 45] and got back [4411306415 | Thapliyal et al. | 2025 | Citations: 111]. The rest were recalled papers, dressed in the same format and missing the tag ("(LLM Memory)" showed up once across 11 reports). Plain numeric IDs cured the missing W, not the wrong labels.

You know every label you sent, so the check is a set difference:

import re
sent = set(labels_in_prompt)                      # exactly as you formatted them
cited = set(re.findall(r"\[([^\[\]]+)\]", report))
unknown = cited - sent                            # flag before a human reads it

Two cleanups belong there too. Each report opens with an empty block, the slot Qwen3 models reserve for reasoning when that mode is enabled (turning it off was not part of our test). And the per-section summaries use slightly different markers than the prompt requests.

What the 95.5% does not tell you

The score proves each reference exists, not that claims are correct. We did not compare each sentence with its excerpt, yet drift turned up anyway. One report gave a paper 25 citations instead of 27, seven times over. Another turned "one eighth" of a cost into "1/4 cost". Ai2 flags the same weakness: the right study, cited for more than it found. Have a person review figures taken from excerpts.

The test was small: 4 questions, 15 OpenAlex abstracts each, inputs around 5,000 tokens. Ai2's quality score (87.0 out of 100, against 77.3 for plain Qwen3-8B) covers computer science questions only. We graded none of the reports, and ran no head-to-head against another model.

For the retrieval side, see our EmbeddingGemma 2 post on multimodal search. The full AstaBrief-8B write-up with the vLLM command, SDK example and per-request timings also has the complete citation tally.

Credit: Ai2's Asta team built, trained, evaluated and released AstaBrief and its prompt, using reports from Anthropic, OpenAI and DeepSeek models, with GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek-R1 as graders. The Qwen team made Qwen3-8B, the vLLM project serves it unchanged, Hugging Face hosts the weights, OpenAlex supplied the abstracts, and an AI Search video pointed us to the release. Our part: the SDK example, the run on our own cloud, the counting. Read the complete AstaBrief-8B report on inferencekey.com before you wire it into your stack.

title: logsloth reads the failing CI log so I don't have to
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

I'm Anand Biju. I built logsloth, a small command line tool for the most boring part of my week: a red CI run.

The red X is never the bad part. The bad part is opening the log. You get a few hundred lines of checkout, cache restore, dependency install and cleanup, and somewhere in the middle is the one line that matters. The last line, Process completed with exit code 1, tells you nothing. So you scroll, you search for "error", you hit forty false matches, and ten minutes later you find out a package was missing.

logsloth does that scrolling. Give it a log file, pipe a command into it, or point it at a failed GitHub Actions run:

logsloth ci.log
npm test 2>&1 | logsloth
logsloth --gh https://github.com/owner/repo/actions/runs/1234567890

It prints a short card with four lines. CULPRIT is the real error line. WHERE is the file and line. WHY is one sentence on what went wrong. FIX is the next thing to do. Below that are the handful of log lines it used as evidence, with their original line numbers, so you can check it instead of trusting it. --md prints the same thing as Markdown for a PR comment, and --json is there for scripts.

Demo

These are all real runs on my machine. The first three use real logs from public projects, pulled with gh run view --log-failed.

A ruff-format pre-commit failure in psf/requests. The log is 284 lines and the run ends with about forty lines of git cleanup after the error. logsloth skips that and lands on the hook that failed:

A mypy error in pallets/flask. The error message wraps over three lines, and logsloth joins them back together:

A failing vitest assertion in vitejs/vite. The log is 653 lines. Here Gemma got distracted by a pnpm store prune line in the excerpt and suggested running it. The validator threw that out, and the card shows the built-in hint instead. The footer says so.

And one of the bundled examples, a pytest run where httpx was never installed:

Code

Anandb71 / logsloth

Reads a failing CI log so you don't have to. Code finds the evidence, a local Gemma explains it.

logsloth

A small CLI that reads a long failing CI, test, or build log and tells you the one thing that broke.

Code finds the evidence and states the facts. A local open-weight model (gemma3:1b via Ollama) only explains why it failed and suggests a fix. The model never sees the whole log.

Why

When CI goes red you get a few hundred lines of setup, cache restores, and cleanup, with the real error somewhere in the middle. Finding it is boring and you do it many times a week. logsloth does the scrolling for you and runs entirely on your machine, so private logs never leave it.

Install

pip install -e .

You also need Ollama and the default model:

ollama pull gemma3:1b

OLLAMA_HOST defaults to http://127.0.0.1:11434.

Usage

# a log file
logsloth path/to/ci.log
# piped from a local command
npm test 2>&1 | logsloth

# a failed
…
View on GitHub
ollama pull gemma3:1b
python3 -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate
pip install -e .
logsloth examples/pytest_httpx.log

python -m pytest -q runs 47 tests. They never call the model or the network.

How I Built It

The rule I followed: code finds the facts, the model only explains them.

My first version let Gemma 3 1B write everything. It went badly. On a cargo error it wrote the literal text "one sentence: what broke" as the culprit. On a jest log it pointed at the test file instead of the file that was missing the import. On the real flask and requests logs it blamed git config and safe.directory, because the cleanup lines at the end of a GitHub log look like errors. That third one is why I stopped testing only on my own example logs.

So the work is split.

Triage is plain Python. It strips ANSI colours, including the literal ^[[36m that gh run view --log-failed leaves in, plus the timestamps and the jobstep prefix on every line. It folds repeated lines and then scores lines against known failure patterns: Python tracebacks and pytest E lines, Cannot find module, rust error[E...] with its --> location, mypy and ruff style path:line: error:, pre-commit hooks that print Failed, pip's No matching distribution, docker's failed to solve, and a few more. The final exit code 1 line can never be the main finding if anything else matched. CULPRIT and WHERE come straight from this step, so they are always lines that really are in the log.

Gemma only writes why and fix. It gets a short excerpt, between 6 and 15 lines in the runs above, not the whole log. The prompt only includes the rules that apply to this failure. When I listed every rule at once, the 1B model copied them, and suggested "install httpx using pip or npm".

Every answer gets checked. Why and fix are validated separately. They have to be non-empty and short. They can't repeat the prompt or the example. They can't tell a git story when the failure isn't about git. They have to name the real package, symbol or hook. If the fix says to install something, that name has to appear in the log. That check caught Gemma telling me to "include lodoc" when the log said lodash. A field that fails is replaced by a built-in hint for that error type, and the footer says which parts came from the model and which from the hint, for example why from gemma3:1b, fix from hint.

In my final runs over the seven logs, Gemma's why was kept in six and its fix in three. On the vite log both fields fell back to hints. On this shared, CPU-only box a call took between 1.9 and 34 seconds, and most were around 10.

It is standard-library Python. Ollama serves the model over HTTP on localhost. I built it this week with the Cursor CLI agent doing a lot of the typing, while I wrote the spec, ran it against real logs, and kept tightening the validator.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

CI logs are full of things you shouldn't paste into a hosted chatbot: internal hostnames, paths, package names from a private registry, sometimes a token someone forgot to mask. With an open-weight model on my own machine, the log stays here. Nothing gets uploaded, there's no API key to manage, and running it a hundred times a day costs nothing.

It also changed how I built it. A 1B model running locally is fast and cheap enough to call on every failure, but it is wrong often enough that I had to treat its output as a suggestion to check, not an answer. Because I control the prompt, the temperature, the retry and the validation, I could build that checking around it. Swapping in a different model is one flag, --model.

The Lazy Payoff

Before: open the run, expand the failed step, scroll past setup, search for "error", skip the false matches, find the real line, then work out which file it means.

After: logsloth --gh . I read four lines, then check the evidence lines if I don't believe them. On the 653-line vite log the card had the failing spec file and line, and the expected and received values, in the evidence block. I didn't have to open the log.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. logsloth runs Gemma 3 1B (gemma3:1b) locally through Ollama. It writes the why and fix, and the validator decides which of its answers to keep.

title: Snooze Desk: a local Gemma reads my GitHub notifications while I sleep
summary:
This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 3: Slow and Steady

What I Built

I have a confession. Most mornings I open GitHub, see the notification count, and close the tab. Then I feel guilty about it all day. Somewhere in that pile is a person waiting on my review, sitting right next to three dependency bumps and someone offering me free stars.

So I built Snooze Desk, a lazy developer's overnight desk.

While I sleep, it does the boring part:

  • A durable Temporal workflow pulls my GitHub notifications.
  • A local Gemma model running in Ollama sorts each one into needs-you, can-wait or ignore.
  • For the ones that need me, it drafts a reply that quotes real details from the notification, like the line number in a stack trace or the number of changed components in a PR.
  • It writes a short morning digest, so the first thing I read is three lines, not forty tabs.

In the morning I open one dark screen. Red means something needs my attention. Green means it is handled. For each draft I can approve, edit, reject or snooze. Snoozing starts a Temporal durable timer with a live countdown, and the item comes back when the timer fires. The timer lives in Temporal, not in a browser tab.

Who gets to be lazier: anyone with a noisy GitHub inbox. During Hacktoberfest, that is probably you.

Demo

Code

RockingThor / snooze-desk

Lazy developer's overnight desk: local Gemma, Temporal and Sentry triage your GitHub notifications while you sleep. DEV Hacktoberfest 2026 entry.

Snooze Desk 🌙

The lazy developer's overnight desk — Process GitHub notifications with local AI while you sleep.

A Hacktoberfest 2026 Open-Source AI Challenge project (Week 3: "Slow and Steady").

What It Does

Snooze Desk runs a durable Temporal workflow that processes your GitHub notifications overnight using a local Gemma model. Wake up to:

  • A 3-line morning digest summarizing what needs your attention
  • Smart classification: needs-you (red), can-wait (gray), or ignore
  • AI-drafted replies for issues and PRs that need a response
  • One-click actions: approve, edit, snooze, or reject each draft
  • Durable snoozing: workflow sleeps for hours or days, survives restarts

Everything runs locally. Your notifications never leave your machine. Zero API costs.

Why Open-Source AI?

  1. Privacy: All processing happens on your laptop. No data leaves your machine.
  2. Zero cost: No API keys, no usage fees. Run it forever for free.
  3. Offline-capable: Works without internet…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The stack is Next.js for the desk, the Temporal TypeScript SDK for the overnight job, Ollama running Gemma for the thinking, Octokit for GitHub, and Sentry for tracing every model call.

Temporal does the waiting

The whole night is one Temporal workflow. Fetching notifications, classifying each one, writing the digest and posting an approved reply are all activities. That matters because a local model is a flaky dependency. With Temporal, a failed step gets retried, and the workflow picks up where it left off instead of starting over.

Snooze is a Temporal timer too. When I say "not now", the workflow just sleeps. It is the most relatable code I have ever written.

Gemma does the sorting

The classifier sends each notification to Gemma and asks for strict JSON back. My first prompt was simple. It turned out to be too simple, and Sentry is how I found out.

Sentry shows me what actually happened

Every model call is a Sentry span with op ai.inference, named classify_notification or generate_digest_summary. Each span carries the model name, the prompt version, input and output token counts, Ollama's load and eval durations, and the Temporal workflow id and attempt number. The Ollama HTTP call shows up as a child span.

On October 22 I did 7 live runs on a Linux box with 8 CPU cores and no GPU. I used six sample notifications that I know the right answers for: three that need me, a dependency bump and a friendly praise thread that can wait, and one spam message. Sentry accepted every envelope, 54 out of 54.

Here is what the traces told me:

Model Prompt Classify mean ms, min to max Input tokens, mean Output tokens, mean Tokens per second Digest ms Correct
gemma3:1b v1 1734, 1502 to 2081 215 71 44.3 1390 3 of 6
gemma3:1b v2 2926, 2417 to 3276 351 88 45.9 1991 3 of 6
gemma4:e4b v1 58123, 41556 to 71342 222 428 7.8 56679 5 of 6
gemma4:e4b v2 49195, 37485 to 65936 358 414 8.8 53766 6 of 6

Finding one: the small model says yes to everything. gemma3:1b is fast, under 3 seconds per notification on CPU. It also labelled all six notifications needs-you. That includes one titled "FREE GITHUB STARS! Click here now!!!". So it scored 3 of 6, and only because three of them really did need me.

I assumed my prompt was bad, so I wrote a v2:

  • clear rules for each label, including "spam stays ignore even when it mentions you"
  • five few shot examples

title: I moved 432 Cowork tasks to a new Claude account. Claude Code deleted 13 of my transcripts on the way.
summary:
This week I retired one Claude account and moved to another on the same Mac. The old account had 432 Cowork tasks, 10 Projects, 39 scheduled tasks, 26 memory files and 28 Claude Code sessions. The account data export covers chats. I couldn't find a way to export what Cowork keeps on the machine: Projects, project memory and scheduled tasks.

So I went looking on disk. Everything was there. Three things still went wrong, and one of them cost me data. The scripts I wrote along the way are now a small open-source tool, carryover.

Where things live

None of this is documented. It's what the macOS desktop app wrote through October 2026.

What Where
Claude Code sessions ~/.claude/projects//.jsonl
Claude Code memory ~/.claude/projects//memory/*.md
Cowork tasks ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/local-agent-mode-sessions///local_.json (metadata) and local_/audit.jsonl (transcript)
Cowork task output local_/outputs/
Cowork Projects spaces.json (name, folders, instructions) and spaces//memory/
Cowork global memory agent/memory/
Scheduled tasks scheduled-tasks.json, with each prompt in ~/Documents/Claude/Scheduled//SKILL.md

Claude Code history isn't tied to the login. On the same machine, the new account can claude --resume an old session and carry on. Cowork is per account: the new account starts with an empty sidebar, no Projects and no scheduled tasks.

Problem 1: Claude Code deletes old transcripts

Halfway through the move, Claude Code started once and 13 of my transcripts disappeared. All of them were from September 19 to 21.

It's a setting. The data usage docs say Claude Code keeps transcripts in ~/.claude/projects/ for 30 days by default, and cleanupPeriodDays changes that. I had never set it. (Sessions started from the desktop app or Cowork are exempt by default.)

My last Time Machine backup was from May. The only copy left is a local snapshot macOS took on October 9. If you use Claude Code from the terminal, add this to ~/.claude/settings.json today, whether or not you plan to switch accounts:

{ "cleanupPeriodDays": 3650 }

Problem 2: rebuilt tasks can't read their own prompts

The 39 scheduled tasks keep their prompts as files under ~/Documents/Claude/Scheduled/. I recreated the tasks in the new account and pointed them at those files, then found the tasks couldn't open them. Cowork treats ~/Documents/Claude as its own folder and keeps sessions out of it.

The fix was dull: copy all 62 prompt folders (39 registered, 23 that no task pointed at any more) to a normal folder and point the tasks there. Also, 12 of the 39 had been moved to the cloud by the app in September and October. Those cloud copies stay with the old account and need rebuilding like the rest.

Problem 3: transcripts are full of secrets

My first idea was to copy the whole Cowork folder somewhere safe. Then I opened a metadata file. Each one also holds the full system prompt, connector configs with server URLs, and the tools I had approved. You don't want that in a backup you might share.

The transcripts were worse. When I ran the finished tool on my own data, it masked 78 strings. 52 of them were API keys and bearer tokens, most inside curl and docker run -e commands from debugging sessions months ago. They had been sitting in plain-text JSON the whole time. If you have used Cowork or Claude Code for a while, assume the same about yours, and rotate whatever you find.

The tool

carryover does two things.

carryover scan lists what is on disk and warns about the three problems above: how many transcripts the 30-day cleanup will take this week, which prompts live under ~/Documents/Claude, which folders no longer exist, and which tasks were already moved to the cloud. It writes nothing.

carryover export ~/somewhere builds a folder you can open in any editor:

  • condensed transcripts (your prompts and Claude's replies, no tool noise) for every Claude Code session and Cowork task
  • memory, global and per project
  • Cowork output files, copied as-is
  • one RESTORE.md per Project: name, folders, instructions, and a first message for the new Project that tells Claude to read the old memory, check it against the current state of the folders, and keep only what still holds
  • TASKS.md with every scheduled task's schedule, folders, last run and prompt
  • INDEX.md and a manifest.json that records every file written and every file skipped

On my machine, without output files, the export took 9 seconds and wrote 1,198 files. Recreating a Project from its restore pack is four pastes.

A few rules I held it to. It only opens source files for reading, and it refuses an output folder inside any source folder. It reads 12 named fields from session metadata and ignores the rest. It never copies files that look like credentials (.env, *.pem, id_rsa, cookie stores) and never opens ~/.claude.json. It masks common key formats in everything it writes. Masking is a safety net, not a guarantee, so read the archive before you share it.

It's Python 3.9+, standard library only, MIT licensed:

pipx install git+https://github.com/lizhuojunx86/carryover
carryover scan

What it can't carry

Logins and connector sign-ins, plugins, and anything that only lived in the cloud: claude.ai Project documents, chat history, cloud scheduled tasks and their run logs. For those, request the old account's data export while you can still sign in. Export the old account's memory as well. Mine held newer Project notes than the local files: 12 of the 63 files that existed in both places had changed since the last local copy.

If you're about to switch

Set cleanupPeriodDays first. Run carryover scan and read the warnings before you sign out of anything. Then export, rebuild Projects from the restore packs, and recreate scheduled tasks with their prompts in a folder Cowork can read.

I've only tested this on macOS and Linux with a personal account. If your layout looks different (Windows, Team or Enterprise), open an issue with your carryover scan --json output, private bits removed, and I'll add support. Happy to answer questions in the comments.

title: Teaching an AI assistant to forget a deleted Stripe customer
summary:
Here is a small billing horror story.

A customer asks to be deleted. Someone clicks delete in Stripe. A week later your AI assistant is still happily telling people what that customer pays and which invoice is open. It sounds completely sure. It is completely wrong.

Nothing crashed. The assistant just kept a memory of something that no longer exists.

I wanted to fix that for Stripe. So for Mergetober I built a connector for Cognee. The code lives in PR #394 for issue #4547.

Billing data is a good test for a connector. Nothing in it stands alone. A charge belongs to an invoice, an invoice to a subscription, a subscription to a customer. If a connector loses those links, the assistant loses the story.

What it does

Cognee turns documents into a knowledge graph that an agent can search. The connector feeds it from Stripe. It reads customers, subscriptions, invoices, charges, products and disputes. Then:

  • Every object becomes a short document.
  • Related objects stay connected. A customer, its subscription, the invoice, the charge and the dispute can all be reached from each other.
  • Later runs read only what changed.
  • Anything you delete in Stripe is forgotten. 
await cognee.remember(
    stripe_source(),  # key and account come from the environment
    dataset_name="stripe",
    primary_key="id",
    write_disposition="merge",
)

It never reads card numbers or payment methods. Each document is built from a short list of allowed fields, not from the raw object. A field Stripe adds next year cannot sneak in by accident. Email, phone and metadata are off unless you ask for them.

Two choices I changed my mind about

Links. My plan was to treat Stripe rows as a relational table and let Cognee build the links from foreign keys. Then I checked. The staging tables dlt writes to SQLite have no foreign keys at all, even when you declare them. So the links would never appear.

The fix was simpler. Every document lists the things it belongs to: customer:cus_..., subscription:sub_..., product:prod_.... Cognee stores those as shared nodes. Two documents that share a node are connected. No guessing, and no model involved.

Changes. Stripe's list calls can only filter by creation date. That sounds fine until someone pays an old invoice. The invoice was created last month, so a date filter never sees it again.

So later runs read Stripe's events instead. One request asks what happened since last time. Then only the objects named in those events are fetched again. If nothing happened it costs one request. If the events are older than Stripe keeps them, the connector lists everything again and compares.

The real test

First I tested against a fake Stripe. 62 tests, no network. But a fake only proves what you thought to fake.

So I made a free Stripe test account, seeded it with three customers, and gave the connector a read-only key that can look but not touch.

The first sync took in 25 objects across all six types and Cognee built the graph with OpenAI. I asked which customers have unpaid invoices. The answer was Charliecorp, with an open invoice for $120.00. I asked which customers have a disputed charge and what plan they are on. It followed the trail from the dispute to the charge to the customer to the subscription to the plan and answered fraudulent, needs response, Pro plan at $49 a month.

Then I synced again without changing anything. One request. Nothing written.

Then I renamed a customer and deleted another straight from the Stripe dashboard. The next sync made three requests, wrote one object and forgot one. The deleted customer vanished from the documents and from the graph. The renamed one showed up under its new name.

That is the behaviour I wanted.

The bug only a real account could find

My first real run printed every charge without a link to its invoice.

My fake Stripe gave charges an invoice field. The real one does not. In the API version I pin (2025-03-31) a charge no longer says which invoice it paid. Instead the invoice lists its payments, and you have to ask for them. My tests passed on imaginary data and missed it completely.

The fix links the two through the payment they share. The invoice and the charge now both belong to the same payment_intent node. The fake now behaves like the real thing, so a test would catch this next time. A review pass flagged a second risk. A dispute's events name only the dispute, so the charge's disputed flag could go stale. The connector now refreshes the charge too.

Try it

The seed script and the example live in packages/connector/stripe/. Stripe's test mode is free and needs no business verification. Create a restricted key with read access, run the seed once, then rename and delete things in the dashboard between runs.

If you point it at your own account I would love to hear what breaks.

So later runs read Stripe's events instead. One request asks what happened since last time. Then only the objects named in those events are fetched again. If nothing happened it costs one request. If the events are older than Stripe keeps them, the connector lists everything again and compares.

The real test

First I tested against a fake Stripe. 62 tests, no network. But a fake only proves what you thought to fake.

So I made a free Stripe test account, seeded it with three customers, and gave the connector a read-only key that can look but not touch.

The first sync took in 25 objects across all six types and Cognee built the graph with OpenAI. I asked which customers have unpaid invoices. The answer was Charliecorp, with an open invoice for $120.00. I asked which customers have a disputed charge and what plan they are on. It followed the trail from the dispute to the charge to the customer to the subscription to the plan and answered fraudulent, needs response, Pro plan at $49 a month.

Then I synced again without changing anything. One request. Nothing written.

Then I renamed a customer and deleted another straight from the Stripe dashboard. The next sync made three requests, wrote one object and forgot one. The deleted customer vanished from the documents and from the graph. The renamed one showed up under its new name.

That is the behaviour I wanted.

The bug only a real account could find

My first real run printed every charge without a link to its invoice.

My fake Stripe gave charges an invoice field. The real one does not. In the API version I pin (2025-03-31) a charge no longer says which invoice it paid. Instead the invoice lists its payments, and you have to ask for them. My tests passed on imaginary data and missed it completely.

The fix links the two through the payment they share. The invoice and the charge now both belong to the same payment_intent node. The fake now behaves like the real thing, so a test would catch this next time. A review pass flagged a second risk. A dispute's events name only the dispute, so the charge's disputed flag could go stale. The connector now refreshes the charge too.

Try it

The seed script and the example live in packages/connector/stripe/. Stripe's test mode is free and needs no business verification. Create a restricted key with read access, run the seed once, then rename and delete things in the dashboard between runs.

If you point it at your own account I would love to hear what breaks.

title: Winter Boot: Spring Boot-style microservices in PHP 8.5
summary:
If you have used Spring Boot, you already know most of Winter Boot.

In an earlier job I was writing Spring Boot and PHP side by side. Spring Boot hooked me. You could start implementing right away, dependency injection just worked, and convention over configuration meant the code I wrote was my app logic and little else. Microservices came together fast. So I kept asking myself: why can't we do this in PHP? I made the first commit in February 2021 to find out.

Winter Boot is an open-source framework for writing microservices in PHP 8.5. It takes the Spring Boot programming model (beans, dependency injection, declarative transactions, caching, scheduling) and maps it onto PHP attributes. There is no XML and no code generation step.

This post is a short tour, not a manual. The full documentation covers everything else, and the code is on GitHub.

A small service

Here is a service that reads a product from Postgres and caches it:


namespace com\example\shop;

use dev\winterframework\cache\stereotype\CacheEvict;
use dev\winterframework\cache\stereotype\Cacheable;
use dev\winterframework\pdbc\PdbcTemplate;
use dev\winterframework\stereotype\Autowired;
use dev\winterframework\stereotype\Service;
use dev\winterframework\txn\stereotype\Transactional;

#[Service]
class ProductService {
    #[Autowired]
    private PdbcTemplate $db;

    #[Cacheable(cacheNames: 'products')]
    public function find(int $id): array {
        return $this->db->queryForMap(
            'SELECT * FROM products WHERE id = ?', 
            [$id]
        );
    }

    #[Transactional]
    #[CacheEvict(cacheNames: 'products', allEntries: true)]
    public function rename(int $id, string $name): void {
        $this->db->update(
            'UPDATE products SET name = ? WHERE id = ?',
            [$name, $id]
        );
    }
}

And a controller that exposes it (imports trimmed from here on):

#[RestController]
class ProductController {
    #[Autowired]
    private ProductService $products;

    #[GetMapping(path: '/products/{id}')]
    public function get(#[PathVariable] int $id): ResponseEntity {
        return ResponseEntity::ok()->withJson($this->products->find($id));
    }
}

The entry point is one class:

require_once __DIR__ . '/vendor/autoload.php';

#[EnableCaching]
#[EnableTransactionManagement]
#[WinterBootApplication(
    configDirectory: [__DIR__ . '/config'],
    scanNamespaces: [['com\\example\\shop', __DIR__ . '/src']]
)]
class ShopApplication {
    public static function main(): void {
        (new WinterWebSwooleApplication())->run(self::class);
    }
}

ShopApplication::main();

Plus a few lines of application.yml:

server:
    port: 8080

datasource:
    -   name: shopdb
        isPrimary: true
        url: "pgsql:host=localhost;dbname=shop"
        username: shop
        password: "*****"

Run php ShopApplication.php, then curl localhost:8080/products/1. That's the whole app.

How it runs

At boot the framework scans your namespaces, builds the bean graph and maps routes. This happens once per worker process, not per request. The server underneath is Swoole, so the process stays alive and the context stays in memory between requests. You pay the reflection and wiring cost up front, and request handling is just method calls.

#[Transactional] and #[Cacheable] are aspects. They wrap the method call without a generated proxy class. A small native PHP extension (winter_boot) handles the interception. That extension is required, which is one more thing to install. I think it's worth it. There are no proxy files to regenerate after a deploy, and final classes still work. The official Docker image ships with it already built, so in practice most people never compile it.

The rest of the box

The parts I end up using in almost every service:

  • PdbcTemplate for plain SQL
  • PPA (PHP Persistence API), a lightweight ORM: mark a class with #[Table], add PpaEntityTrait, and the framework writes the INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE for you. The Doctrine module is there if you need a full ORM.
  • #[Transactional] with propagation, rollback rules and multiple datasources
  • #[Scheduled] and #[Async] for background work, no separate cron or queue runner
  • A built-in migrator for plain .sql files, easy to run as a pre-deploy step
  • Actuator endpoints for health and info, plus Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry
  • Interceptors, CORS, coroutine-safe sessions

Optional modules cover Redis, Kafka, SQS, S3, OpenSearch and service discovery. You add a module through Composer and enable it in application.yml. Most of them live in winter-modules, and Doctrine ORM and DBAL support is in winter-doctrine.

One newer piece I like: put #[McpTool] on a controller method or a service method and it is served as a Model Context Protocol tool on /mcp. The input schema comes from the PHP signature and PHPDoc. So the same endpoint your frontend calls can be called by Claude or any other MCP client, through the same interceptors and auth.

Does it hold up?

The most demanding thing running on it right now is Snowprint, a self-hosted, cookie-less web analytics tool. In its benchmark it stores about 9,900 events per second on 2 CPUs and about 19,800 on 4 CPUs, with every accepted event persisted. It uses the parts shown above: REST controllers, PdbcTemplate, scheduled rollups, migrations and the actuator. It also tracks traffic on the Winter Boot docs site.

Rough edges

Winter Boot needs PHP 8.5, Swoole and the winter_boot extension. That is a narrower setup than a typical PHP-FPM host, and shared hosting is out. It is built for containers. If you deploy with Docker, use suvera/winter-boot as the base image and the extension problem goes away.

It is also a smaller project than Laravel or Symfony. The ecosystem is the framework plus its own modules, not thousands of third-party packages. Plain Composer libraries work fine, though, since it's still PHP.

Try it 

composer require suvera/winter-boot

The easiest way to run it is the official Docker image, suvera/winter-boot. It's built on php:8.5-cli-alpine and comes with every extension the framework needs, plus Redis, Kafka and PostgreSQL drivers, already installed. There is also suvera/winter-boot-mysql if you're on MySQL. The installation guide shows a ready-to-use Dockerfile.

  • Docs: https://suvera.github.io/winter-boot/
  • Source: https://github.com/suvera/winter-boot
  • Docker image: https://hub.docker.com/r/suvera/winter-boot
  • Example service: https://github.com/suvera/winter-example-service

Issues and pull requests are welcome. If you build something with it, I'd like to hear about it.

title: Building the MyZubster Metaverse: Realtime Infrastructure, Security, Reliability, and What Comes Next
summary:
Building the MyZubster Metaverse: Realtime Infrastructure, Security, Reliability, and What Comes Next

The MyZubster Metaverse is evolving from an experimental interactive environment into a more structured, observable, and production-oriented platform.

Our goal is not simply to render a virtual world. We are building an open-source environment where authenticated users, guests, communities, developers, and AI-assisted experiences can interact through traceable and reliable services.

During the latest development phase, we focused on the foundations that must exist before adding more ambitious WebXR, social, and multiplayer features:

  • authenticated metaverse sessions;
  • server-authorized world actions;
  • realtime communication;
  • distributed abuse protection;
  • privacy-safe observability;
  • MongoDB and Redis readiness;
  • Preview infrastructure isolated from Production;
  • automated tests and continuous evidence;
  • explicit operational and security gates.

This article describes what we implemented, the architectural decisions behind it, what we verified, and what still needs to happen before production rollout.

1. From client-controlled actions to authenticated sessions

One of the most important changes was moving world actions away from implicit client trust.

A browser must not be able to claim an arbitrary user identity or perform a privileged action simply by sending a crafted request.

The current architecture binds metaverse actions to authenticated session credentials. The server is responsible for determining:

  • which user is connected;
  • which role the user has;
  • which session or community the action belongs to;
  • whether the requested operation is permitted;
  • whether the submitted identity matches the authenticated principal.

This creates a clear trust boundary:


text
Browser input
    ↓
Authenticated HTTP or realtime session
    ↓
Server-side identity and authorization checks
    ↓
Validated world action
    ↓
Persistent or realtime state update
Client state can still improve the user experience, but it is no longer treated as authoritative security evidence.
2. Realtime access tokens
We introduced a dedicated token endpoint for the realtime subsystem.
An authenticated application session can request a short-lived realtime token. The token contains only the minimum information required by the gateway, such as:
- user identifier;
- authorized role;
- optional public username;
- correlation identifier;
- expiration time.
The response also describes the supported connection contract:
{
  "success": true,
  "expiresInSeconds": 300,
  "socketPath": "/realtime",
  "transports": ["websocket", "polling"],
  "namespaces": [
    "user:{id}",
    "community:{id}",
    "session:{id}"
  ]
}
The correlation identifier lets us connect an HTTP request, token-minting operation, socket connection, and later operational events without exposing sensitive application data.
3. Authorized realtime channels
Realtime communication is organized around explicit channel families:
user:{id}
community:{id}
session:{id}
These channels are not arbitrary rooms that a client can join freely.
The server validates whether the authenticated user may enter the requested channel. This is essential for preventing:
- cross-user subscription;
- unauthorized community access;
- session impersonation;
- client-generated room escalation;
- accidental data leakage between realtime contexts.
We are also separating connection authorization from application events. Establishing a socket connection does not automatically authorize every action that may travel through it.
4. Redis-backed distributed presence
A single-process memory map is useful during local development, but it is not sufficient for a horizontally scaled realtime service.
When multiple application instances are running, each instance sees only its own connected users. A reconnect or deployment can also destroy local presence state.
We therefore implemented a Redis-backed presence store.
Redis keeps short-lived connection records for users inside community and session channels. The implementation supports:
- adding a connection;
- refreshing its expiration;
- removing it during disconnection;
- listing active members;
- handling multiple sockets belonging to the same user;
- pruning expired records;
- detecting the first and last active connection.
Presence data uses a TTL. Stale sockets eventually disappear even when the application does not receive a clean disconnect event.
The service retains a local fallback to avoid completely breaking realtime behavior during a Redis incident. However, that fallback is considered degraded mode—not production-ready distributed presence.
5. Redis failure handling
Redis operations are wrapped with explicit failure handling.
When Redis initialization or an established operation fails, the service:
1. records an aggregate Redis failure;
2. emits a structured operational event;
3. invalidates the failed shared client;
4. falls back locally where permitted;
5. exposes the degraded state through readiness.
We deliberately avoid returning Redis connection strings, internal exception messages, usernames, or infrastructure details to public clients.
Operational errors are represented through safe categories such as:
{
  "event": "redis_presence_failure",
  "operation": "health",
  "status": "local_fallback",
  "mode": "local-fallback",
  "reason": "redis_error"
}
6. Distributed rate limiting
Metaverse actions and realtime endpoints need protection against abuse, spam, and accidental request storms.
Local counters are insufficient when traffic reaches multiple server instances, so we developed a distributed rate-limiting path using Redis.
The rate-limiting architecture is designed to support:
- authenticated user limits;
- guest or anonymous limits;
- action-specific policies;
- shared counters across instances;
- explicit retry metadata;
- privacy-safe operational metrics;
- controlled degraded behavior.
Rate limiting is part of the server-side authorization boundary. A client cannot reset its allowance by refreshing the page or connecting to a different application instance.
7. Privacy-safe observability
Operational visibility is necessary, but observability must not become a second surveillance system.
The realtime metrics endpoint is restricted to administrators and exposes aggregate counters rather than individual user activity.
Current metrics can describe behavior such as:
- connection attempts;
- successful connections;
- authorization failures;
- active connection changes;
- Redis failures;
- rate-limit decisions;
- service degradation.
The endpoint does not return raw tokens, Redis URLs, database credentials, private messages, or individual browsing histories.
A simplified response follows this pattern:
{
  "success": true,
  "privacy": "aggregate-only",
  "counters": {
    "connectionAttempts": 42,
    "connectionSuccesses": 40,
    "redisFailures": 0
  }
}
The response uses Cache-Control: no-store so operational data is not retained by shared caches.
8. A real production-readiness endpoint
We added a public readiness endpoint:
GET /api/realtime/health
Its purpose is different from a generic “the process is running” check.
The endpoint verifies whether the dependencies required by the realtime subsystem are actually operational:
- Express router;
- MongoDB connection;
- Redis connection.
A healthy response follows this contract:
{
  "success": true,
  "service": "myzubster-realtime",
  "status": "ready",
  "checks": {
    "router": "ready",
    "mongodb": "connected",
    "redis": "connected"
  },
  "timestamp": "2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z"
}
If MongoDB or Redis is unavailable, the endpoint returns HTTP 503:
{
  "success": false,
  "service": "myzubster-realtime",
  "status": "degraded",
  "checks": {
    "router": "ready",
    "mongodb": "connected",
    "redis": "disconnected"
  }
}
Readiness therefore means more than “the route exists.” It means the service can currently use its required durable and distributed infrastructure.
9. Reusing the shared Redis client
The readiness endpoint does not create a separate Redis implementation.
It uses the same shared Redis client used by the presence store. This reduces the risk of reporting a healthy dependency through one connection while the application is using another broken connection.
The readiness function:
1. checks whether REDIS_URL is configured;
2. initializes or reuses the shared client;
3. sends PING;
4. returns a normalized status;
5. invalidates the client after a failed ping;
6. records the failure through the existing observability service.
Conceptually:
async function redisReadiness() {
  if (!redisConfigured()) {
    return { ready: false, status: "not_configured" };
  }

  const client = await getRedis();

  if (!client) {
    return { ready: false, status: "disconnected" };
  }

  try {
    await client.ping();
    return { ready: true, status: "connected" };
  } catch (error) {
    recordRedisFailure(error);
    invalidateRedisClient(client);

    return { ready: false, status: "disconnected" };
  }
}
10. Isolated Preview infrastructure
We did not reuse Production database credentials for branch deployments.
Instead, the Vercel Preview environment was connected to isolated resources:
- a dedicated MongoDB Preview database;
- a scoped MongoDB Preview user;
- a Redis resource connected through REDIS_URL;
- environment variables restricted to Preview.
This gives us a safer environment for testing readiness, presence, failure modes, and migrations.
The boundary is explicit:
Pull request branch
    ↓
Vercel Preview deployment
    ↓
Preview-only MongoDB
    ↓
Preview-only Redis
Production secrets were not copied into the branch environment, and Production was not changed during this phase.
11. Automated verification
We added tests at two levels.
Presence-store tests
The Redis presence tests verify that the service:
- reports Redis as connected after a successful ping;
- reports it as disconnected after a failed ping;
- records an alertable Redis failure;
- falls back locally when connection initialization fails;
- falls back when an established Redis operation fails.
HTTP route tests
The realtime route tests verify:
- HTTP 200 when MongoDB and Redis are ready;
- HTTP 503 when MongoDB is disconnected;
- HTTP 503 when Redis is disconnected;
- the presence of the expected readiness fields;
- Cache-Control: no-store;
- the absence of sensitive values;
- administrator-only access to aggregate metrics;
- denial of metrics access to regular users.
The main CI workflow completed successfully, including:
- backend lint;
- backend unit tests;
- frontend unit tests;
- backend build;
- frontend build;
- artifact generation.
The Seller Free policy regression workflow also passed, and the Continuous Evidence Gate produced a retained evidence artifact.
12. Current pull-request status
The readiness work is tracked in a Draft pull request.
The latest implementation includes:
- Redis readiness in the shared presence service;
- Redis gating in the public health endpoint;
- MongoDB and Redis degradation behavior;
- unit and route-level tests;
- successful Preview deployment.
The pull request remains Draft intentionally.
We have not merged it and have not performed a Production rollout.
13. The current security blocker
The latest security audit detected two dependency advisories:
- one high-severity vulnerability;
- one moderate-severity vulnerability.
The affected package is ip-address <= 10.7.3, and an updated version is available.
This dependency issue is separate from the Redis readiness implementation, but it is still a release gate. The lockfile and the transitive dependency path must be reviewed and updated in a focused security change.
We will not describe the branch as release-ready while a high-severity dependency audit is failing.
14. What is still missing
The core realtime foundation is substantially stronger, but MYZ-83 is not complete.
The remaining work includes the following.
Dependency remediation
Upgrade the vulnerable dependency path, regenerate the lockfile, rerun the complete audit, and verify that the change does not break network-address handling.
Load baseline
Measure the realtime system under repeatable workloads:
- concurrent socket connections;
- connection and reconnection bursts;
- channel joins and leaves;
- presence refresh operations;
- distributed rate-limit operations;
- token issuance;
- HTTP and socket latency;
- MongoDB and Redis resource consumption.
The result must include reproducible commands, environment information, and retained metrics.
Redis restart drill
We need to demonstrate what happens when Redis becomes unavailable and later returns:
Redis healthy
    ↓
Redis interrupted
    ↓
Readiness becomes degraded
    ↓
Failures are counted
    ↓
Local fallback is bounded
    ↓
Redis reconnects
    ↓
Readiness returns to ready
MongoDB restart drill
The same operational evidence is required for MongoDB:
- health transition;
- connection retry behavior;
- public response safety;
- recovery time;
- absence of credential leakage;
- final healthy state.
Multi-instance validation
Distributed presence and rate limiting must be tested with multiple application instances. A single-instance test cannot prove that Redis-backed coordination behaves correctly across replicas.
Reconnection behavior
We still need repeatable tests for:
- short network interruptions;
- token expiration;
- reconnect storms;
- duplicate sockets;
- stale presence cleanup;
- retry backoff;
- client state restoration.
Production smoke test
Production verification will happen only after:
1. security remediation;
2. completed review;
3. explicit merge authorization;
4. an approved deployment;
5. confirmation that the correct Production resources are configured.
No Production change should be inferred from the successful Preview work.
15. What comes after reliability
Once the operational foundation is accepted, we can continue with higher-level metaverse features:
- richer shared-world interactions;
- realtime community events;
- persistent avatars and progression;
- WebXR exploration;
- spatial interfaces;
- collaborative missions;
- verified contributor identities;
- connections between the Metaverse and MyZubster Knowledge;
- development requests linked to GitHub contributions;
- community-governed experiences;
- optional reward and bounty bridges backed by verifiable evidence.
The sequence matters.
WebXR and visual features are valuable, but authentication, authorization, abuse protection, distributed state, and recovery behavior must come first.
Conclusion
The latest MyZubster Metaverse work is primarily about trustworthiness.
We moved closer to a system where:
- identities are derived from authenticated sessions;
- world actions are authorized by the server;
- realtime channels have explicit access rules;
- presence and rate limits can work across multiple instances;
- Redis and MongoDB are part of the readiness contract;
- operational metrics remain aggregate and privacy-safe;

event_model_payload.summary:
Building the MyZubster Metaverse: Realtime Infrastructure, Security, Reliability, and What Comes Next

The MyZubster Metaverse is evolving from an experimental interactive environment into a more structured, observable, and production-oriented platform.

Our goal is not simply to render a virtual world. We are building an open-source environment where authenticated users, guests, communities, developers, and AI-assisted experiences can interact through traceable and reliable services.

During the latest development phase, we focused on the foundations that must exist before adding more ambitious WebXR, social, and multiplayer features:

  • authenticated metaverse sessions;
  • server-authorized world actions;
  • realtime communication;
  • distributed abuse protection;
  • privacy-safe observability;
  • MongoDB and Redis readiness;
  • Preview infrastructure isolated from Production;
  • automated tests and continuous evidence;
  • explicit operational and security gates.

This article describes what we implemented, the architectural decisions behind it, what we verified, and what still needs to happen before production rollout.

1. From client-controlled actions to authenticated sessions

One of the most important changes was moving world actions away from implicit client trust.

A browser must not be able to claim an arbitrary user identity or perform a privileged action simply by sending a crafted request.

The current architecture binds metaverse actions to authenticated session credentials. The server is responsible for determining:

  • which user is connected;
  • which role the user has;
  • which session or community the action belongs to;
  • whether the requested operation is permitted;
  • whether the submitted identity matches the authenticated principal.

This creates a clear trust boundary:


text
Browser input
    ↓
Authenticated HTTP or realtime session
    ↓
Server-side identity and authorization checks
    ↓
Validated world action
    ↓
Persistent or realtime state update
Client state can still improve the user experience, but it is no longer treated as authoritative security evidence.
2. Realtime access tokens
We introduced a dedicated token endpoint for the realtime subsystem.
An authenticated application session can request a short-lived realtime token. The token contains only the minimum information required by the gateway, such as:
- user identifier;
- authorized role;
- optional public username;
- correlation identifier;
- expiration time.
The response also describes the supported connection contract:
{
  "success": true,
  "expiresInSeconds": 300,
  "socketPath": "/realtime",
  "transports": ["websocket", "polling"],
  "namespaces": [
    "user:{id}",
    "community:{id}",
    "session:{id}"
  ]
}
The correlation identifier lets us connect an HTTP request, token-minting operation, socket connection, and later operational events without exposing sensitive application data.
3. Authorized realtime channels
Realtime communication is organized around explicit channel families:
user:{id}
community:{id}
session:{id}
These channels are not arbitrary rooms that a client can join freely.
The server validates whether the authenticated user may enter the requested channel. This is essential for preventing:
- cross-user subscription;
- unauthorized community access;
- session impersonation;
- client-generated room escalation;
- accidental data leakage between realtime contexts.
We are also separating connection authorization from application events. Establishing a socket connection does not automatically authorize every action that may travel through it.
4. Redis-backed distributed presence
A single-process memory map is useful during local development, but it is not sufficient for a horizontally scaled realtime service.
When multiple application instances are running, each instance sees only its own connected users. A reconnect or deployment can also destroy local presence state.
We therefore implemented a Redis-backed presence store.
Redis keeps short-lived connection records for users inside community and session channels. The implementation supports:
- adding a connection;
- refreshing its expiration;
- removing it during disconnection;
- listing active members;
- handling multiple sockets belonging to the same user;
- pruning expired records;
- detecting the first and last active connection.
Presence data uses a TTL. Stale sockets eventually disappear even when the application does not receive a clean disconnect event.
The service retains a local fallback to avoid completely breaking realtime behavior during a Redis incident. However, that fallback is considered degraded mode—not production-ready distributed presence.
5. Redis failure handling
Redis operations are wrapped with explicit failure handling.
When Redis initialization or an established operation fails, the service:
1. records an aggregate Redis failure;
2. emits a structured operational event;
3. invalidates the failed shared client;
4. falls back locally where permitted;
5. exposes the degraded state through readiness.
We deliberately avoid returning Redis connection strings, internal exception messages, usernames, or infrastructure details to public clients.
Operational errors are represented through safe categories such as:
{
  "event": "redis_presence_failure",
  "operation": "health",
  "status": "local_fallback",
  "mode": "local-fallback",
  "reason": "redis_error"
}

Metaverse actions and realtime endpoints need protection against abuse, spam, and accidental request storms.
Local counters are insufficient when traffic reaches multiple server instances, so we developed a distributed rate-limiting path using Redis.
The rate-limiting architecture is designed to support:
- authenticated user limits;
- guest or anonymous limits;
- action-specific policies;
- shared counters across instances;
- explicit retry metadata;
- privacy-safe operational metrics;
- controlled degraded behavior.
Rate limiting is part of the server-side authorization boundary. A client cannot reset its allowance by refreshing the page or connecting to a different application instance.
7. Privacy-safe observability
Operational visibility is necessary, but observability must not become a second surveillance system.
The realtime metrics endpoint is restricted to administrators and exposes aggregate counters rather than individual user activity.
Current metrics can describe behavior such as:
- connection attempts;
- successful connections;
- authorization failures;
- active connection changes;
- Redis failures;
- rate-limit decisions;
- service degradation.
The endpoint does not return raw tokens, Redis URLs, database credentials, private messages, or individual browsing histories.
A simplified response follows this pattern:
{
  "success": true,
  "privacy": "aggregate-only",
  "counters": {
    "connectionAttempts": 42,
    "connectionSuccesses": 40,
    "redisFailures": 0
  }
}
The response uses Cache-Control: no-store so operational data is not retained by shared caches.

We added a public readiness endpoint:
GET /api/realtime/health
Its purpose is different from a generic “the process is running” check.

- Express router;
- MongoDB connection;
- Redis connection.

{
  "success": true,
  "service": "myzubster-realtime",
  "status": "ready",
  "checks": {
    "router": "ready",
    "mongodb": "connected",
    "redis": "connected"
  },
  "timestamp": "2026-10-23T00:00:00.000Z"
}

  "success": false,
  "service": "myzubster-realtime",
  "status": "degraded",
  "checks": {
    "router": "ready",
    "mongodb": "connected",
    "redis": "disconnected"
  }
}

2. initializes or reuses the shared client;
3. sends PING;
4. returns a normalized status;
5. invalidates the client after a failed ping;
6. records the failure through the existing observability service.

async function redisReadiness() {
  if (!redisConfigured()) {
    return { ready: false, status: "not_configured" };
  }

  const client = await getRedis();

  if (!client) {
    return { ready: false, status: "disconnected" };
  }

  try {
    await client.ping();
    return { ready: true, status: "connected" };
  } catch (error) {
    recordRedisFailure(error);
    invalidateRedisClient(client);

    return { ready: false, status: "disconnected" };
  }
}

- a dedicated MongoDB Preview database;
- a scoped MongoDB Preview user;
- a Redis resource connected through REDIS_URL;
- environment variables restricted to Preview.
This gives us a safer environment for testing readiness, presence, failure modes, and migrations.
The boundary is explicit:
Pull request branch
    ↓
Vercel Preview deployment
    ↓
Preview-only MongoDB
    ↓
Preview-only Redis
Production secrets were not copied into the branch environment, and Production was not changed during this phase.
11. Automated verification
We added tests at two levels.
Presence-store tests
The Redis presence tests verify that the service:
- reports Redis as connected after a successful ping;
- reports it as disconnected after a failed ping;
- records an alertable Redis failure;
- falls back locally when connection initialization fails;
- falls back when an established Redis operation fails.
HTTP route tests
The realtime route tests verify:
- HTTP 200 when MongoDB and Redis are ready;
- HTTP 503 when MongoDB is disconnected;
- HTTP 503 when Redis is disconnected;
- the presence of the expected readiness fields;
- Cache-Control: no-store;
- the absence of sensitive values;
- administrator-only access to aggregate metrics;
- denial of metrics access to regular users.
The main CI workflow completed successfully, including:
- backend lint;
- backend unit tests;
- frontend unit tests;
- backend build;
- frontend build;
- artifact generation.
The Seller Free policy regression workflow also passed, and the Continuous Evidence Gate produced a retained evidence artifact.
12. Current pull-request status
The readiness work is tracked in a Draft pull request.
The latest implementation includes:
- Redis readiness in the shared presence service;
- Redis gating in the public health endpoint;
- MongoDB and Redis degradation behavior;
- unit and route-level tests;
- successful Preview deployment.
The pull request remains Draft intentionally.
We have not merged it and have not performed a Production rollout.
13. The current security blocker
The latest security audit detected two dependency advisories:
- one high-severity vulnerability;
- one moderate-severity vulnerability.
The affected package is ip-address <= 10.7.3, and an updated version is available.
This dependency issue is separate from the Redis readiness implementation, but it is still a release gate. The lockfile and the transitive dependency path must be reviewed and updated in a focused security change.
We will not describe the branch as release-ready while a high-severity dependency audit is failing.
14. What is still missing
The core realtime foundation is substantially stronger, but MYZ-83 is not complete.
The remaining work includes the following.
Dependency remediation
Upgrade the vulnerable dependency path, regenerate the lockfile, rerun the complete audit, and verify that the change does not break network-address handling.
Load baseline
Measure the realtime system under repeatable workloads:
- concurrent socket connections;
- connection and reconnection bursts;
- channel joins and leaves;
- presence refresh operations;
- distributed rate-limit operations;
- token issuance;
- HTTP and socket latency;
- MongoDB and Redis resource consumption.
The result must include reproducible commands, environment information, and retained metrics.
Redis restart drill
We need to demonstrate what happens when Redis becomes unavailable and later returns:
Redis healthy
    ↓
Redis interrupted
    ↓
Readiness becomes degraded
    ↓
Failures are counted
    ↓
Local fallback is bounded
    ↓
Redis reconnects
    ↓
Readiness returns to ready
MongoDB restart drill
The same operational evidence is required for MongoDB:
- health transition;
- connection retry behavior;
- public response safety;
- recovery time;
- absence of credential leakage;
- final healthy state.
Multi-instance validation
Distributed presence and rate limiting must be tested with multiple application instances. A single-instance test cannot prove that Redis-backed coordination behaves correctly across replicas.
Reconnection behavior
We still need repeatable tests for:
- short network interruptions;
- token expiration;
- reconnect storms;
- duplicate sockets;
- stale presence cleanup;
- retry backoff;
- client state restoration.
Production smoke test
Production verification will happen only after:
1. security remediation;
2. completed review;
3. explicit merge authorization;
4. an approved deployment;
5. confirmation that the correct Production resources are configured.
No Production change should be inferred from the successful Preview work.
15. What comes after reliability
Once the operational foundation is accepted, we can continue with higher-level metaverse features:
- richer shared-world interactions;
- realtime community events;
- persistent avatars and progression;
- WebXR exploration;
- spatial interfaces;
- collaborative missions;
- verified contributor identities;
- connections between the Metaverse and MyZubster Knowledge;
- development requests linked to GitHub contributions;
- community-governed experiences;
- optional reward and bounty bridges backed by verifiable evidence.
The sequence matters.
WebXR and visual features are valuable, but authentication, authorization, abuse protection, distributed state, and recovery behavior must come first.
Conclusion
The latest MyZubster Metaverse work is primarily about trustworthiness.
We moved closer to a system where:
- identities are derived from authenticated sessions;
- world actions are authorized by the server;
- realtime channels have explicit access rules;
- presence and rate limits can work across multiple instances;
- Redis and MongoDB are part of the readiness contract;
- operational metrics remain aggregate and privacy-safe;
- Preview infrastructure is isolated from Production;
- CI produces reproducible technical evidence;
- known security failures remain visible instead of being hidden.
The Metaverse is not production-complete yet, but its foundation is becoming measurable, testable, and independently reviewable.
That is the kind of progress we want: not unsupported claims, but small engineering steps backed by code, tests, deployments, and evidence.

title: Your AI bot should remember like Git — designing persistent, Git-backed memory for personal agents
summary:
Most AI assistants have a memory problem that has nothing to do with model quality:

  • You can't see what they remember.
  • You can't fix it when it's wrong.
  • You can't roll it back when an update makes it worse.
  • You definitely can't diff it.

We ran into this while building personal agent bots — bots that live with you for months, develop a role (researcher, writer, engineer), chat in your group channels, and run scheduled jobs while you're away. For a bot like that, "memory" isn't a nice-to-have embedding trick. It's the bot's long-term state, and long-term state deserves the same treatment we give source code: files you can read, history you can inspect, and versions you can restore.

So in DeepSeekBot — an open-source (MIT) Grok Bot alternative that runs as a plugin on DeepSeek Harness — each bot's memory is not a vector database or a hidden server-side profile. It's an ordinary Git repository.

This post is about why we did that, how it works in practice, and the trade-offs we'd warn you about if you copied the idea.

What "Git-backed memory" actually means

Each bot has its own memory working tree: plain files (Markdown) that hold what the bot knows about you, your projects, and its own role. As conversations happen, the bot updates those files. Because the memory is a Git repo, you get, for free:

  • A working diff. Uncommitted memory changes are grouped (new memories vs. updates to existing ones) and shown as diffs you can read before they're part of the bot's history — in the same way you'd review a pull request.
  • A commit history. Every memory change lands as a commit. You can click any commit and see exactly which files changed and how, and load older history as far back as the bot has existed.
  • Branches. A branch is an alternate line of how the bot's memory evolves. You can branch from an older commit ("from here, remember things differently") without destroying what came after on the original branch.
  • Named versions. Any commit can be given a human-readable name, stored as a Git tag — "the draft before the big tidy-up" — so the restore points that matter are findable months later, not buried in a hash list.
  • Restore. You can restore the memory to the state of any earlier commit. If there's uncommitted work in the way, it's first saved as its own commit, so restoring never silently deletes anything.
  • Automatic backups. Memory changes, the end of a conversation, and any restore operation all trigger a backup, including uncommitted files.

And the most practical consequence: push the memory repo to GitHub, and the same bot — same identity, same memory — can live on more than one machine. Clone it at the office and at home, and it's the same colleague in both places.

Why not just embeddings?

Embeddings are great for recall ("find the snippet about X"). They're bad at accountability.

Question a user actually asks Vector store Git repo of files
"What do you remember about me?" Nothing inspectable Open the files and read
"That's wrong, fix it." Re-embed and hope Edit the file, commit
"You were better last week. Go back." Not really possible Restore a tagged commit
"Why do you think that?" Opaque similarity A diff, with a date
"Move my bot to another PC." Export/import tooling git push / git clone

We still think semantic recall has its place for retrieval inside a conversation. But the source of truth for a long-lived bot should be something a human can audit with tools they already trust. Developers already know how to review a diff; nobody knows how to review 4,096 floats.

The design rules this forced on us

Working with Git as the memory substrate imposed some useful discipline:

  1. Memory writes are changes, not mutations. The bot doesn't silently rewrite its state; changes accumulate as reviewable diffs and commits. The UI literally separates "current uncommitted changes" from "committed history."

  2. Human overrides are first-class. Because memory is files, a user correction is just an edit. The bot can be wrong and be fixed, not argued with.

  3. Every escape hatch gets a safety net. Restore is scary, so restore itself is a commit, pre-restore state is auto-committed, and full-folder backups happen before a backup-restore. You can be bold with history when going back is itself safe.

  4. Vocabulary matters. In the product UI, most people never see raw Git terms — changes are grouped as "new memory" vs "memory updates," and only if you flip a setting do the labels switch to unstaged/staged/untracked. Same repo, two mental models.

The honest trade-offs

  • Your host has to be awake. DeepSeekBot runs on your own machine via DeepSeek Harness; if the computer is off, your bots aren't working. Git memory doesn't solve availability — it solves trust.
  • Remote models still see context. Memory lives on your host, but when a bot calls a remote model provider (you configure your own in Harness — it's not DeepSeek-only), the relevant context goes to that provider. Local memory is not the same as local inference.
  • Files don't scale infinitely. A bot that remembers everything forever will accumulate a big repo. Named versions, branches, and the occasional human tidy-up are features of the model, not afterthoughts — but you do have to design for pruning.
  • Non-technical users meet Git concepts. Most never need them, and the UI hides them — but power users asking for "undo for memory" are really asking for Git whether they know it or not.

Try it / steal the idea

DeepSeekBot is MIT-licensed and installable from the DeepSeek Harness desktop app (Plugins → Add plugin → deepseekbot@1.4.1):

  • GitHub: https://github.com/BotHarness/DeepSeekBot
  • Product & docs: https://deepseekbot.app/en/

Each bot also has its own identity and persona, can be @-mentioned in group chats with other bots, can be reached in Slack, Discord, Feishu/Lark, QQ and WeChat, and can create its own scheduled tasks ("every morning at 9, send me a log digest" is a sentence, not a settings page). But honestly, the piece we'd most like other agent builders to copy is the boring one:

State you can diff is state you can trust.

If you're building agents with long-term memory — Git-backed or not — I'd love to hear how you're handling inspection, correction, and rollback in the comments.

title: Kaeso
summary:
A long time has passed since I last worked on a personal project which I worked on solely by myself, and whenever I did, I learned an enormous amount by doing so. Today I will be presenting my plans for Kaeso, an open source AI Gateway which will initially aim to compete with LiteLLM and then move on by adapting new features. My goal is to build a foundation for the future, and by building Kaeso this is the perfect way. I personally love and believe in open source because without it, I would definitely not be where I am right now.

From my understanding and knowledge of market needs, I believe that this idea is not a good one and will probably fail, at least as a startup it would. This project in its current state is a solved problem and the initial user base will be very small as LiteLLM is significantly further developed.

Kaeso in its first version will be split into four core components which will shape its fundamental structure:

As Apple's early Marketing Philosophy said, people DO judge a book by its cover. So the first big difference will be the UX/UI for the people using Kaeso. In my view, the current LiteLLM User Interface has considerable room for a cleaner and more cohesive experience. Kaeso will aim to create a good environment for all kinds of users.

Of course, announcing this as the only change is vague. In most cases nobody cares about the UI and it's the functionality which matters, but as I'm currently just trying to establish a baseline, this is the first and best visible best practice I can create.

Lastly, I want to mention that the Kaeso Roadmap will be fully led by me and that will probably remain the case at its core.
