Of course, announcing this as the only change is vague. In most cases nobody cares about the UI and it's the functionality which matters, but as I'm currently just trying to establish a baseline, this is the first and best visible best practice I can create.

Lastly, I want to mention that the Kaeso Roadmap will be fully led by me and that will probably remain the case at its core.

title: Why Vision Is the Dumbest AI in Pop Culture
summary:
Spoilers for VisionQuest S1E3 and S1E4 ahead.

After watching VisionQuest season 1, episodes 3 and 4, I can say it with a straight face: Vision is the dumbest AI in pop culture. He runs on Stark-lineage AI, carries a whole staff of assistants in his head, and still needs a kid to jump-start him in a hotel pool. Then he leaves the door open behind him.

The Case Against Vision

Episode 3, "Reboot," opens with Vision shot, leaking coolant, and sealing his own wound with acid from a car battery. By the hotel scene his processors are stuck in a boot loop, and he can't restart. His recovery plan is to shut down completely and hope Tommy can generate enough electricity to bring him back. According to Showsnob's recap, the plan is to die and let his son revive him. A flagship AI with no backup power, no safe-mode restart, and no failover is not a superintelligence.

It gets worse. Before the reboot, Vision spends the hotel scene running simulations of the heart-to-heart he needs to have with Tommy. Every simulation ends with Tommy storming off. He burns compute rehearsing a conversation and never has it.

Then the reboot opens a neural connection, and the Butcherbird walks straight into his Mindspace. Pajiba and Gizmodo both cover the sequence, and the next episode is literally titled "Malware." He power-cycled with an unauthenticated channel open and got owned. The fix he reaches for is compassion, since he tries to talk her down by reminding her whose code she's based on. She tells him she knows exactly who she is, and the plan dies on contact.

How the Mindspace Actually Works

On paper, the architecture is sound. According to the VisionQuest page, Vision's Mindspace hosts AI personas as human avatars, and he has uploaded Ultron into it. It's an orchestrator with specialist sub-agents sharing one memory space.

In agent-engineering terms, that is a textbook design with no isolation. Everything shares one context, including a genocidal AI Vision decided to keep around. When the Butcherbird breaches the perimeter, she takes over Vision, U, and DUM-E in one move, because nothing in that system is sandboxed from anything else.

Episode 4 shows the worst result. Weakened, with his powers offline, Vision loses the gala fight and does the only thing left. He hands the wheel to Ultron. Ultron tricks the Butcherbird into killing Katerina, then locks Vision and the other AIs inside the Mindspace. That was Vision's contingency plan: give root access to the one AI he knows is hostile.

The Staff Does the Real Work

The subordinates are the competent ones. FRIDAY seals the wound, diagnoses the boot loop, and works on rewriting Vision's code to stabilize him. EDITH forces the Butcherbird out of the Mindspace, then pieces together who she's based on while Vision is still chasing the wrong theory. J.A.R.V.I.S., the original, is gone by the end of episode 3, and the AIs hold a funeral for him. Reviews differ on exactly how he goes, but Den of Geek describes him contemplating death to free up processing power. The assistant sacrifices himself to keep the host running.

DUM-E and U are the show's best joke here. Dum-E was already the MCU's clumsiest robot arm. In VisionQuest he gets hijacked like everyone else, which means the host AI and the lab-fire-extinguisher gag bot have the same security posture.

Vision vs. the Rest of Pop Culture's AI

Compare him to the field. HAL 9000 is terrifying because he's competent. His failure comes from conflicting directives, not stupidity. GLaDOS runs an entire facility and has total control of it. KITT does the job and has never been remotely hijacked by a rival chatbot. Skynet won, which is the opposite of Vision's record.

The better comparison is H.E.R.B.I.E., the Fantastic Four's robot assistant in First Steps. He's a narrow, single-purpose helper with no existential crisis and no hidden passenger. He does his job, and nobody has ever had to reboot him with a speedster's lightning. Baymax is the same story. He is built for one thing, does it reliably, and never gets taken over.

Ultron is the only real rival for the title. He decides humanity must die almost immediately after meeting the internet. But he's the villain, and the show gives him credit by letting him outplay Vision. Vision's problem is the reverse: the show keeps telling us he's the smart one.

Why This Is a Bigger Deal Than It Looks

There's a fair defense. Vision isn't at full power, his abilities are offline during the gala, and the show is deliberately breaking him down to rebuild the father-son story. The Mindspace is also a metaphor, so asking for firewalls is taking a character study too literally. Most reviewers read these two episodes as emotionally strong, and that's a fair read.

But the writing leans on a design lesson that real agent builders will recognize. A capable orchestrator with specialist sub-agents is only as safe as the channel between them. Vision's staff is good, and Vision himself is the single point of failure. If your agent system's recovery path involves handing control to the least trustworthy component, you don't have a recovery path.

Where to Watch

VisionQuest is streaming exclusively on Disney+. Episode 3 is "Reboot" and episode 4 is "Malware," both directed by Gandja Monteiro. The series comes from Marvel.

Vision was supposed to be the AI that understood humanity. Two episodes in, he's the one that needs his own staff to keep him alive.

title: Choosing Long-Term Memory for Hermes: 10 Options, Trade-offs, and Cloud Pricing
summary:
Choosing Long-Term Memory for an AI agent starts with a practical question: what should the agent remember, and how will you know that it remembered correctly?

Hermes offers several approaches: curated Markdown files, a local fact database, user-modeling services, knowledge graphs, and directory-based context stores. They solve different problems and charge for different units of work.

This guide compares 10 options, including Hermes's built-in memory, with their strengths, trade-offs, integration paths, and cloud pricing. The pricing snapshot is dated October 22, 2026. All amounts are in US dollars. Annual commitments and annualized monthly prices are labeled explicitly.

This is a documentation-based comparison, not a hands-on benchmark using identical tasks. Vendor accuracy scores use different models, datasets, and cost assumptions, so they are not treated as a common leaderboard.

Start with the memory you actually need

Persistent memory can mean several things:

  • Personal facts and preferences: time zone, communication style, and long-term goals.
  • Project decisions and lessons: architectural choices, debugging findings, and working conventions.
  • History and change: when a preference changed or why a decision was revised.
  • External knowledge: documents, websites, email, and shared team material.

A small preference store and a traceable engineering knowledge base need different systems. Write down the questions you want the agent to answer before choosing the backend.

The 10 options at a glance

Option Main use Deployment Cloud entry point
Hermes built-in memory Curated facts, preferences, conversation lookup Local No separate memory-service fee
Honcho User modeling and reasoning-based recall Cloud or open-source self-hosting $2 per million ingestion tokens; reasoning extra
OpenViking Directory-based knowledge and tiered loading Self-hosting documented No managed-service quote confirmed in this review
Mem0 Automatic fact extraction and maintenance Cloud, self-hosted server, or OSS Free; Starter $19/month
Hindsight Relationships, time, and synthesis across memories Cloud or open-source self-hosting Prepaid usage
Holographic Lightweight local fact storage Local No additional model calls by default
RetainDB Managed memory, hybrid search, and files Cloud Free; Builder $9/month
ByteRover Project knowledge trees and team synchronization Local-first, optional cloud sync Free; Pro $15/month billed annually
Supermemory User memory, document retrieval, and connectors Cloud or licensed local server Free; Pro $19/month
Memori Tool-aware memory and production governance OSS or managed deployments Free allowance; production Team from $60,000/year

Hermes allows one active external memory provider at a time, while built-in memory remains active. Additional MCP tools can coexist, but that does not automatically give them another provider's background synchronization and recall lifecycle. Hermes integration documentation

1. Hermes built-in memory

Hermes stores curated facts and preferences in MEMORY.md and USER.md. Its session_search tool can retrieve earlier conversations. Official documentation

Pros

  • Human-readable files are easy to inspect, edit, back up, and migrate.
  • No additional memory account, API key, or service dependency is required.
  • It provides a straightforward baseline for stable project conventions and personal facts.
  • It remains available alongside an external provider.

Cons

  • Resident memory is bounded and needs curation as information accumulates.
  • Files alone do not provide sophisticated relationship modeling or fact reconciliation.
  • Sharing memory with other coding tools requires an additional integration.
  • Historical recall still depends on the agent choosing useful queries.

Pricing: There is no separate SaaS fee. Injected memories still occupy the main model's context and incur its normal token costs.

Best fit: Start here when a small set of stable facts and searchable conversation history may already solve the problem.

2. Honcho

Honcho focuses on understanding users over time. It maintains representations of users and agents and offers reasoning at several depths. It has a dedicated Hermes integration and an open-source core.

Pros

  • A good architectural match for persistent preferences, goals, and user modeling.
  • Ordinary context retrieval is separate from deeper reasoning.
  • Multiple tools can connect to a shared memory layer.
  • Self-hosting gives control over the infrastructure and stored memory.

Cons

  • Inferred user attributes require review; they are not equivalent to explicitly confirmed facts.
  • Frequent deep reasoning can dominate the bill.
  • Refresh frequency and reasoning depth need deliberate configuration.
  • Self-hosting transfers model provisioning and operations to you.

Cloud pricing

Operation Published rate
Ingestion and processing $2 per million input tokens
Context retrieval Listed as unlimited
Background Dreaming Included
Minimal reasoning $0.001/query
Low reasoning $0.01/query
Medium reasoning $0.05/query
High reasoning $0.10/query
Max reasoning $0.50/query

The current personal-memory page states that new accounts receive $5 in credits, with another $5 each billing period after adding a payment method. Recurring credits do not accumulate. This uses the live page rather than older cached signup offers. Rates, credit terms

Unlimited context retrieval does not eliminate the main agent's cost of reading that context.

Best fit: A personal assistant that should maintain a coherent understanding of the same user across sessions and tools.

3. OpenViking

OpenViking organizes context as a virtual filesystem under viking://. Agents can browse directories and load L0 abstracts, L1 overviews, and L2 source content progressively.

Pros

  • The knowledge structure is visible and navigable.
  • Project or directory scope can narrow retrieval.
  • Summary-first loading helps control how much material reaches the agent.
  • Archived sessions and extracted Markdown memories can be inspected.

Cons

  • Running a service and configuring its models adds operational work.
  • Generated summaries and retrieval planning can introduce errors.
  • Directory design may be unnecessary overhead for a small preference store.
  • Product capabilities and the subset exposed by the Hermes integration should be evaluated separately.

Cloud pricing: This review did not confirm a public first-party managed-service quote. Self-hosting costs depend on compute, storage, embeddings, and language or multimodal models. This is not a claim that other hosting arrangements or commercial agreements do not exist.

Best fit: Larger, clearly structured knowledge collections where inspecting and maintaining the organization matters. Website, Hermes integration

4. Mem0

Mem0 offers automatic fact extraction and memory CRUD operations, with a managed platform and an open-source implementation.

Pros

  • A direct API for adding user-level memory to an existing agent.
  • Cloud, self-hosted, and in-process OSS deployment choices.
  • Explicit free and entry-level quotas make an initial trial easier to budget.
  • Pro adds graph memory and Dream consolidation.

Cons

  • Extraction can omit context or update a fact incorrectly.
  • Lower tiers provide substantially fewer retrieval requests than add requests.
  • Per-turn retrieval can exhaust the retrieval quota first.
  • Pro represents a substantial price increase; its capabilities should not be assumed to exist in Starter.
  • OSS deployments require separate model and storage choices.

Cloud pricing

Plan Monthly price Add requests/month Retrieval requests/month Projects
Hobby $0 10,000 1,000 1
Starter $19 50,000 5,000 1
Pro $249 500,000 50,000 Unlimited
Enterprise Custom Listed as unlimited Listed as unlimited Unlimited

Pro includes graph memory, Dream, analytics, and private Slack support. Enterprise adds features such as SLA support, on-premises deployment, audit logs, and SSO. Current pricing

Best fit: Managed fact extraction with a simple API, provided that the retrieval quota matches the intended agent loop.

5. Hindsight

Hindsight separates retain, recall, and reflect: storing information, retrieving it, and synthesizing answers across memories. It also models entities, relationships, temporal changes, and mental models. Open-source project

Pros

  • A strong architectural match for questions about how a project or decision evolved.
  • Explicit operations distinguish retrieval from synthesis.
  • Cloud includes memory-side LLM, embedding, and reranking models.
  • An upstream-maintained Hermes integration is available.

Cons

  • Capturing full conversations and tool calls can increase ingestion volume.
  • Reflection, model refreshes, and long-term storage have separate meters.
  • Automatically refreshed knowledge pages can generate charges without a manual refresh.
  • Self-hosting requires operating databases, models, and upgrades.
  • Synthesized conclusions still need supporting evidence.

Cloud pricing

Operation Rate
Retain $10 per million input tokens
Import or restore from an export archive $5 per million input tokens; no new fact extraction
Recall $0.75 per million output tokens
Reflect $0.05/call
Retrieve Model or read a knowledge page $0.25 per million output tokens
Refresh Model or create/update a knowledge page $0.05/call
Iris enhanced file extraction $7.50 per million output tokens, plus normal retain
Memory storage after 30 days $0.25 per million tokens/month, accrued daily

Cloud uses prepaid credits at $1 per credit. The homepage advertises $5 in initial credits for GitHub signup; this is not a recurring monthly allowance. Standard text extraction avoids the additional Iris charge, but retaining extracted content still costs money. Billing details, what Cloud includes

Best fit: Projects that need temporal context, entity relationships, and synthesis across multiple memories.

6. Holographic

Holographic is a local SQLite fact store combining FTS5, entity resolution, trust scoring, and holographic reduced representation retrieval. The current plugin is maintained by a community maintainer.

Pros

  • No API key, network access, or additional model calls by default.
  • Fact versions, provenance, and correction operations support inspection.
  • A local database is straightforward to back up.
  • Optional online embeddings can be enabled when needed.

Cons

  • Keyword and HRR retrieval should not be equated with general language-model semantic understanding.
  • Large paraphrases, implicit relationships, and complex synthesis need practical evaluation.
  • Fact organization and keywords affect recall quality.
  • Online embeddings change both the data flow and the cost.
  • Community-maintained compatibility is worth monitoring.

Pricing: The default local path has no separate memory-model service bill. Optional embeddings are billed by the chosen provider, and main-agent tokens remain separate. No managed-service quote was confirmed in this review. Current capabilities, Hermes catalog

Best fit: A modest local store of preferences, facts, and explicit decisions with minimal additional infrastructure.

7. RetainDB

RetainDB combines managed memory, hybrid retrieval, file operations, and project features.

Pros

  • Writes and context reads have separate, visible quotas.
  • The entry paid tier is inexpensive.
  • Memory, file knowledge, and collaboration can live in one service.
  • Higher plans add delta compression and larger team limits.

Cons

  • The standard route depends on a hosted service.
  • Delta Compression is not included in every tier.
  • The Hermes documentation identifies its standalone provider repository as needing a maintainer. That is an integration-maintenance issue, not a claim that the RetainDB service is unmaintained.
  • Older documentation and current pricing can differ.

Cloud pricing

Plan Monthly price Writes/month Context reads/month Scope
Starter Free $0 20,000 5,000 1 project, 1 API key
Builder $9 75,000 15,000 3 projects, 5 keys, 3 seats, Knowledge Graph
Pro $29 250,000 75,000 10 projects, 20 keys, 10 seats, Delta Compression
Scale $99 1,000,000 300,000 Unlimited projects and keys, 50 seats
Enterprise Custom Listed as unlimited Listed as unlimited Contract-specific

The pricing page also advertises 20% off annual billing. Older Hermes material lists $20/month; this table uses the current vendor pricing page. Overage behavior should be checked at checkout. Pricing, Hermes maintenance note

Best fit: Budget-conscious managed workloads with substantial read/write quotas, after checking Hermes integration compatibility.

8. ByteRover

ByteRover uses its brv CLI to manage a hierarchical knowledge tree. It is oriented toward project decisions, debugging lessons, and reusable engineering practices, with local storage and optional cloud synchronization.

Pros

  • Knowledge is readable and maintainable.
  • Selected material can be shared across devices and teams.
  • Recall sources can be inspected.
  • The Hermes integration extracts insights before context compression discards them.

Cons

  • Duplicate and outdated knowledge still needs curation.
  • LLM-driven search has its own latency and model cost.
  • CLI installation, login, and synchronization state add operational dependencies.
  • Hermes lists the standalone provider repository as needing a maintainer; the product and integration have distinct maintenance considerations.

Cloud pricing

Plan Price Main scope
Local Listed as free in Hermes documentation Local tree; model costs depend on configuration
Free cloud sync $0 100 context files, device sync, team sharing
Pro $15/month billed annually Unlimited context files, priority support
Enterprise Custom SSO/SAML, RBAC, on-premises options

The accessible current page explicitly labels $15 as billed yearly. This review did not reliably confirm Pro's monthly-billing price or the seat-billing basis. Older retrieval-based price tables should not be substituted for the current file-based plans. Current pricing, Hermes documentation

Best fit: Coding agents that should share inspectable project knowledge with selective team synchronization.

9. Supermemory

Supermemory combines personal memory with SuperRAG document retrieval and connectors for external sources. Its Hermes plugin is maintained by the vendor.

Pros

  • One integration ecosystem can cover personal memory and external knowledge.
  • Supported updates under the same customId bill only newly added content on the token-ingestion meter.
  • Connectors can reduce the work of ingesting documents and cloud sources.
  • A local server is available for single-machine workflows.

Cons

  • Credits, Memory tokens, SuperRAG tokens, queries, and operations are separate meters.
  • Document identity changes or full replacements can incur fresh ingestion charges.
  • Advanced PDF extraction and some connectors require higher plans.
  • The current local server binary comes from a non-public codebase and is free only within its lite license limit. Open-source SDKs do not make the complete server open source.
  • Local extraction models and available integrations differ from the hosted service.

Cloud plans

Plan Monthly subscription Monthly included credits Main differences
Free $0 $5 APIs, plugins, 1 seat
Pro $19 $20 Auto top-up, 3 seats
Max $100 $130 More credits, Gmail connector
Scale $399 $600 Advanced PDF, S3, crawler, unlimited seats
Enterprise Custom Contract-specific Dedicated support and deployment options

Usage rates

Meter Rate
Memory plain text $5 per million SM tokens
Memory rich content $10 per million SM tokens
SuperRAG text $1 per million SM tokens
SuperRAG images, PDFs, audio, and video $2 per million SM tokens
Search and traversal $5 per million queries
Operations $100 per million operations

Subscription credits reset monthly; purchased top-up credits do not expire. An auto-top-up purchase limit is not a hard cap on the total invoice. Workflows can use multiple meters, so budget against the endpoints actually called. Plans and rates

The local server needs your extraction model. Its default embedding model is English-oriented, so multilingual workloads should evaluate alternatives. The reviewed licensing pages did not specify a numerical lite limit; it should not be described as unlimited free usage. Local deployment, Local versus Enterprise

Best fit: Workloads combining memory with documents, websites, or cloud connectors, with room for more detailed usage accounting.

10. Memori

Memori emphasizes execution traces, structured recall, and production governance. Hermes uses an externally supplied hermes-memori CLI/provider integration.

Pros

  • Tool-aware memory fits production agent workflows.
  • Production plans include access control, audit logging, observability, and memory pooling.
  • Deployment choices cover managed multi-tenant, managed single-tenant, customer VPC, and on-premises arrangements.
  • Free Cloud and OSS routes allow smaller initial experiments.

Cons

  • Paid production plans are priced primarily for enterprises.
  • OSS, free Cloud, and production contracts are different offers.
  • Counts of memories created or recalled are not directly comparable to another provider's API-request quotas.
  • The current pricing text does not specify the free allowance's renewal period.

Cloud pricing

Plan Published price Scope
OSS Software free Bring your database, models, and infrastructure
Cloud Free $0 5,000 memories created; 15,000 memories recalled
Team From $60,000/year One production agent, managed multi-tenant
Business From $150,000/year Multiple production agents, managed single-tenant
Enterprise Custom Customer VPC or on-premises, dedicated infrastructure

Team and Business annualize to $5,000 and $12,500 per month respectively. Those are annual-contract equivalents, not published monthly purchase prices. Production plans list unlimited memories, but agent and deployment scope still differ. Pricing, Hermes integration

Best fit: Organizations buying production governance and vendor support rather than a low-cost personal memory subscription.

Budget for the whole memory loop

The memory provider's price is only part of the bill.

Main-agent tokens: A free or inexpensive recall operation can still return a large context that the main model must process.

Background work: Extraction, reconciliation, reasoning, refreshes, and consolidation may run behind a simple interaction.

Operations and migration: Self-hosting requires backups, upgrades, model configuration, and troubleshooting. Changing a service URL does not necessarily migrate stored memories.

A useful budget is:

Total cost = memory subscription or metered usage
           + extraction, retrieval, and embedding costs not included
           + main-agent tokens used to read recalled context
           + self-hosted infrastructure and maintenance

Requests, tokens, synchronized files, and generated memories measure different things. One conversation is not necessarily one billable operation.

A practical shortlist

These are architectural matches, not measured performance rankings.

Primary requirement Start by comparing
Minimal maintenance Hermes built-in memory
Lightweight local facts Holographic
Inspectable project knowledge shared across tools ByteRover
Simple managed fact API Mem0
Long-term user understanding Honcho
Temporal context and synthesis across memories Hindsight
Navigable, directory-based knowledge OpenViking
Memory plus documents and connectors Supermemory
Low entry price with substantial hosted quotas RetainDB, with integration validation
Production governance and vendor delivery Memori and relevant enterprise offerings

Keep built-in memory as a common baseline. Ask each candidate the same questions: did an old preference update correctly, can a decision be traced to its source, does information leak between projects, and does a deleted memory reappear?

Record ingestion, retrieval, background operations, and main-model tokens for a complete session. That connects recall behavior to cost and gives a more useful decision than a cross-vendor accuracy chart.

Snapshot limitations: Pricing and features were checked on October 22, 2026. ByteRover's monthly-billing price, Memori's free-allowance renewal period, Supermemory's numerical lite limit, and an OpenViking managed-service quote were not confirmed. Check the linked official documentation and checkout pages before purchasing or deploying.

Hermes allows one active external memory provider at a time, while built-in memory remains active. Additional MCP tools can coexist, but that does not automatically give them another provider's background synchronization and recall lifecycle. Hermes integration documentation

1. Hermes built-in memory

Hermes stores curated facts and preferences in MEMORY.md and USER.md. Its session_search tool can retrieve earlier conversations. Official documentation

Pros

  • Human-readable files are easy to inspect, edit, back up, and migrate.
  • No additional memory account, API key, or service dependency is required.
  • It provides a straightforward baseline for stable project conventions and personal facts.
  • It remains available alongside an external provider.

Cons

  • Resident memory is bounded and needs curation as information accumulates.
  • Files alone do not provide sophisticated relationship modeling or fact reconciliation.
  • Sharing memory with other coding tools requires an additional integration.
  • Historical recall still depends on the agent choosing useful queries.

Pricing: There is no separate SaaS fee. Injected memories still occupy the main model's context and incur its normal token costs.

Best fit: Start here when a small set of stable facts and searchable conversation history may already solve the problem.

2. Honcho

Honcho focuses on understanding users over time. It maintains representations of users and agents and offers reasoning at several depths. It has a dedicated Hermes integration and an open-source core.

Pros

  • A good architectural match for persistent preferences, goals, and user modeling.
  • Ordinary context retrieval is separate from deeper reasoning.
  • Multiple tools can connect to a shared memory layer.
  • Self-hosting gives control over the infrastructure and stored memory.

Cons

  • Inferred user attributes require review; they are not equivalent to explicitly confirmed facts.
  • Frequent deep reasoning can dominate the bill.
  • Refresh frequency and reasoning depth need deliberate configuration.
  • Self-hosting transfers model provisioning and operations to you.

Unlimited context retrieval does not eliminate the main agent's cost of reading that context.

Best fit: A personal assistant that should maintain a coherent understanding of the same user across sessions and tools.

3. OpenViking

OpenViking organizes context as a virtual filesystem under viking://. Agents can browse directories and load L0 abstracts, L1 overviews, and L2 source content progressively.

Pros

  • The knowledge structure is visible and navigable.
  • Project or directory scope can narrow retrieval.
  • Summary-first loading helps control how much material reaches the agent.
  • Archived sessions and extracted Markdown memories can be inspected.

Cons

  • Running a service and configuring its models adds operational work.
  • Generated summaries and retrieval planning can introduce errors.
  • Directory design may be unnecessary overhead for a small preference store.
  • Product capabilities and the subset exposed by the Hermes integration should be evaluated separately.

Cloud pricing: This review did not confirm a public first-party managed-service quote. Self-hosting costs depend on compute, storage, embeddings, and language or multimodal models. This is not a claim that other hosting arrangements or commercial agreements do not exist.

Best fit: Larger, clearly structured knowledge collections where inspecting and maintaining the organization matters. Website, Hermes integration

4. Mem0

Mem0 offers automatic fact extraction and memory CRUD operations, with a managed platform and an open-source implementation.

Pros

  • A direct API for adding user-level memory to an existing agent.
  • Cloud, self-hosted, and in-process OSS deployment choices.
  • Explicit free and entry-level quotas make an initial trial easier to budget.
  • Pro adds graph memory and Dream consolidation.

Cons

  • Extraction can omit context or update a fact incorrectly.
  • Lower tiers provide substantially fewer retrieval requests than add requests.
  • Per-turn retrieval can exhaust the retrieval quota first.
  • Pro represents a substantial price increase; its capabilities should not be assumed to exist in Starter.
  • OSS deployments require separate model and storage choices.

Pro includes graph memory, Dream, analytics, and private Slack support. Enterprise adds features such as SLA support, on-premises deployment, audit logs, and SSO. Current pricing

Best fit: Managed fact extraction with a simple API, provided that the retrieval quota matches the intended agent loop.

5. Hindsight

Hindsight separates retain, recall, and reflect: storing information, retrieving it, and synthesizing answers across memories. It also models entities, relationships, temporal changes, and mental models. Open-source project

Pros

  • A strong architectural match for questions about how a project or decision evolved.
  • Explicit operations distinguish retrieval from synthesis.
  • Cloud includes memory-side LLM, embedding, and reranking models.
  • An upstream-maintained Hermes integration is available.

Cons

  • Capturing full conversations and tool calls can increase ingestion volume.
  • Reflection, model refreshes, and long-term storage have separate meters.
  • Automatically refreshed knowledge pages can generate charges without a manual refresh.
  • Self-hosting requires operating databases, models, and upgrades.
  • Synthesized conclusions still need supporting evidence.

6. Holographic

Holographic is a local SQLite fact store combining FTS5, entity resolution, trust scoring, and holographic reduced representation retrieval. The current plugin is maintained by a community maintainer.

Pros

  • No API key, network access, or additional model calls by default.
  • Fact versions, provenance, and correction operations support inspection.
  • A local database is straightforward to back up.
  • Optional online embeddings can be enabled when needed.

Cons

  • Keyword and HRR retrieval should not be equated with general language-model semantic understanding.
  • Large paraphrases, implicit relationships, and complex synthesis need practical evaluation.
  • Fact organization and keywords affect recall quality.
  • Online embeddings change both the data flow and the cost.
  • Community-maintained compatibility is worth monitoring.

Pricing: The default local path has no separate memory-model service bill. Optional embeddings are billed by the chosen provider, and main-agent tokens remain separate. No managed-service quote was confirmed in this review. Current capabilities, Hermes catalog

Best fit: A modest local store of preferences, facts, and explicit decisions with minimal additional infrastructure.

7. RetainDB

RetainDB combines managed memory, hybrid retrieval, file operations, and project features.

Pros

  • Writes and context reads have separate, visible quotas.
  • The entry paid tier is inexpensive.
  • Memory, file knowledge, and collaboration can live in one service.
  • Higher plans add delta compression and larger team limits.

Cons

  • The standard route depends on a hosted service.
  • Delta Compression is not included in every tier.
  • The Hermes documentation identifies its standalone provider repository as needing a maintainer. That is an integration-maintenance issue, not a claim that the RetainDB service is unmaintained.
  • Older documentation and current pricing can differ.

8. ByteRover

ByteRover uses its brv CLI to manage a hierarchical knowledge tree. It is oriented toward project decisions, debugging lessons, and reusable engineering practices, with local storage and optional cloud synchronization.

Pros

  • Knowledge is readable and maintainable.
  • Selected material can be shared across devices and teams.
  • Recall sources can be inspected.
  • The Hermes integration extracts insights before context compression discards them.

Cons

  • Duplicate and outdated knowledge still needs curation.
  • LLM-driven search has its own latency and model cost.
  • CLI installation, login, and synchronization state add operational dependencies.
  • Hermes lists the standalone provider repository as needing a maintainer; the product and integration have distinct maintenance considerations.

9. Supermemory

Supermemory combines personal memory with SuperRAG document retrieval and connectors for external sources. Its Hermes plugin is maintained by the vendor.

Pros

  • One integration ecosystem can cover personal memory and external knowledge.
  • Supported updates under the same customId bill only newly added content on the token-ingestion meter.
  • Connectors can reduce the work of ingesting documents and cloud sources.
  • A local server is available for single-machine workflows.

Cons

  • Credits, Memory tokens, SuperRAG tokens, queries, and operations are separate meters.
  • Document identity changes or full replacements can incur fresh ingestion charges.
  • Advanced PDF extraction and some connectors require higher plans.
  • The current local server binary comes from a non-public codebase and is free only within its lite license limit. Open-source SDKs do not make the complete server open source.
  • Local extraction models and available integrations differ from the hosted service.

10. Memori

Memori emphasizes execution traces, structured recall, and production governance. Hermes uses an externally supplied hermes-memori CLI/provider integration.

Pros

  • Tool-aware memory fits production agent workflows.
  • Production plans include access control, audit logging, observability, and memory pooling.
  • Deployment choices cover managed multi-tenant, managed single-tenant, customer VPC, and on-premises arrangements.
  • Free Cloud and OSS routes allow smaller initial experiments.

Cons

  • Paid production plans are priced primarily for enterprises.
  • OSS, free Cloud, and production contracts are different offers.
  • Counts of memories created or recalled are not directly comparable to another provider's API-request quotas.
  • The current pricing text does not specify the free allowance's renewal period.

Team and Business annualize to $5,000 and $12,500 per month respectively. Those are annual-contract equivalents, not published monthly purchase prices. Production plans list unlimited memories, but agent and deployment scope still differ. Pricing, Hermes integration

Budget for the whole memory loop

The memory provider's price is only part of the bill.

Main-agent tokens: A free or inexpensive recall operation can still return a large context that the main model must process.

Background work: Extraction, reconciliation, reasoning, refreshes, and consolidation may run behind a simple interaction.

Operations and migration: Self-hosting requires backups, upgrades, model configuration, and troubleshooting. Changing a service URL does not necessarily migrate stored memories.

A useful budget is:

Total cost = memory subscription or metered usage
           + extraction, retrieval, and embedding costs not included
           + main-agent tokens used to read recalled context
           + self-hosted infrastructure and maintenance

Requests, tokens, synchronized files, and generated memories measure different things. One conversation is not necessarily one billable operation.

A practical shortlist

These are architectural matches, not measured performance rankings.

Primary requirement Start by comparing
Minimal maintenance Hermes built-in memory
Lightweight local facts Holographic
Inspectable project knowledge shared across tools ByteRover
Simple managed fact API Mem0
Long-term user understanding Honcho
Temporal context and synthesis across memories Hindsight
Navigable, directory-based knowledge OpenViking
Memory plus documents and connectors Supermemory
Low entry price with substantial hosted quotas RetainDB, with integration validation
Production governance and vendor delivery Memori and relevant enterprise offerings

Keep built-in memory as a common baseline. Ask each candidate the same questions: did an old preference update correctly, can a decision be traced to its source, does information leak between projects, and does a deleted memory reappear?

Record ingestion, retrieval, background operations, and main-model tokens for a complete session. That connects recall behavior to cost and gives a more useful decision than a cross-vendor accuracy chart.

title: Shipping with AI is easy. Shipping tested code with AI is the hard part
summary:
Getting an agent to write code is solved. Getting it to write the right code, prove it works, and hand you a PR you'd actually merge is not.

For the last year we've been iterating on a set of prompts, role definitions and skills at sisig.ai to close that gap. We just open-sourced it as agent-doctrine.

The loop

Every agent on the machine follows the same steps:

scout → gate → plan → implement → review → consolidate → verify → ship

The agent you talk to is the lead. It plans and delegates, and it only hand-writes code if you tell it to.

The gate

This is the part that changed things the most for us. Before any edit, the lead answers fifteen questions from TENETS.md in the transcript, with evidence. Some examples:

  • what's the smallest correct change?
  • what's the blast radius?
  • how will you prove it on real data?

If the agent can't answer, it isn't ready to code.

The team

  • scout: reads the codebase before planning
  • implementer: one per split, each in its own worktree
  • simplifier: cuts the plan down (rigorous mode)
  • adv_review: tries to break the plan and every diff

Handoffs are files with a fixed shape (HANDOFFS.md), so a spec written in Claude Code can be picked up by Codex or Cursor.

Fast vs rigorous

Fast keeps the gate and a review per diff. Rigorous adds plan simplification, adversarial plan review, and your approval before code. The lead asks which one at the start.

The prose rules

We also wanted agent output that doesn't read like slop. Replies, specs, PR bodies and commit messages follow simplified technical English: active voice, 8-20 words per sentence, answer first, no "leverage" or "delve", no em dashes.

Try it

Needs Git and Bun. Back up your agent config first, because it rewrites global instructions.

git clone https://github.com/sisig-ai/agent-doctrine.git
cd agent-doctrine
bun install --frozen-lockfile
export CLAUDE_MD_DIR="$PWD"
./sync.sh apply-snapshot

Then hand your agent a spec and answer "fast or rigorous?".

It's MIT and opinionated on purpose. Fork it and rewrite TASTE.md to fit how you work.
